title: Fewer Branches, No Wider Gender Gap: Bank Branch Closures and Women’s Account Ownership and Use in the European Union, 2011–2024
content: Between 2011 and 2024 the number of bank branches per 100,000 adults in the European Union fell by about half. A common concern is that this shift to digital channels excludes groups that rely more on branches, including women. This paper tests that concern with five Global Findex waves for the 27 Member States, measuring the gender gap directly as the male-minus-female difference in account and debit-card ownership. The main finding is a null result: the fall in branch density was not accompanied by a wider gender gap. In fixed-effects estimates, the observed fall implies a change in the account gap of −0.25 percentage points (95% CI −1.78 to 1.27); weighting by sampling variance narrows the interval to −1.25 to 0.67, and equivalence tests reject a widening of one point or more. The result holds in long differences, in stacked fractional models and in wider OECD and European samples. A positive association between branch density and the debit-card gap disappears in log-odds and after correction for multiple testing. By contrast, the gender gap in women’s own digital access is strongly associated with the financial gap (r = 0.70 in 2024). Clustering identifies three regimes, including five Central and Eastern European countries where the gap turned against women, which closed the fewest branches. Machine-learning models cannot predict the gap within the EU. The results are descriptive associations, not causal effects.
